name: Sacrifice for allies
summary: The unit spends a life to lift its team: a cheap minion, one of its own followers, or itself. Whoever stands in the chosen area gets a strong timed buff (less damage taken, more speed, more firepower), and on top of it each receiver may get a bonus of its own kind: ammo back, a repair, a short-lived helper, wider sight or income. The price is real. The minion is gone, the squad is a body short, or the player is out until the next buy. So the questions are whether this moment is worth a life and whether there are lives left to spend. Minions that double as currency have to be kept alive, and that gives the enemy something to hunt.
counterplay: Kill the minions before they are spent: they are cheap and frail, and each one killed is a buff that never happens.
Shoot the offering on its way: a minion has to reach the chosen spot, or stand with the group, before it can give itself up.
Back off for the buff's few seconds, then punish: afterwards the enemy is a body short.
Bait it: a feint that draws the sacrifice early leaves them with nothing for the real push.
Keep receivers out of the area: the buff lands on a place, so zone that place or split the group.
Block the buff where the game allows: in Tempest Rising, infantry under Subjugation can't receive buffs.

other_examples.note: The commander attached to a Guardsmen squad can shoot one of his own men. The squad is a man short, and the troops around him get their morale back and fire twice as fast. Guardsmen cost little and are soon replaced, so the lost man is a small price, and the execution also cuts short the time a broken squad stays broken.

other_examples.note: For some energy the hero kills one chosen model of an allied Guard squad, never a hero, and the rest of that squad deals double damage for a short time. It halts a retreat already under way, and the squad can't retreat until the buff ends. One wargear upgrade adds immunity to suppression and knockback; another lets the same button fall on an enemy trooper instead, which hurts him and cuts his squad's damage.

other_examples.note: Self-sacrifice as a build tool: an Aeon engineer can destroy itself to pour an instant boost into something under construction. Low-tier engineers return a larger share of what they cost than high-tier ones, so the usual offering is an early engineer that has been outgrown, and the wiki rates this above reclaiming it.

shooter_analogues.note: A companion spent for its owner: with this mod fitted, a Sentinel drone brings its downed owner back up and is knocked out itself in exchange. It only fires if it is ranked above the drone's attack behaviours, and the drone is often shot down while it tries.

player_translation.summary: A leader with a few cheap AI followers spends one of them to give the teammates around a chosen spot a strong, short buff; a very cheap unit can spend itself the same way. Every use costs a body, so the player weighs each moment, and the enemy shoots the followers to starve the buff.
as_user: You play a leader with a handful of cheap AI followers (thralls, drones, conscripts). Press Q on a spot and the nearest follower goes there and gives itself up: every teammate in the ring gets a strong buff for several seconds.
Followers are your ammunition: each one spent is one body fewer around you, and they come back slowly or cost money.
You judge the moment. One life for a push that takes the point is a good trade; one life for a buff nobody uses is a waste.
In the spend-yourself version the unit is very cheap: hold Q, the unit is used up, you go back to the buy screen, and your team gets a bigger buff. You score for what the buffed teammates then do.
Teammates can ask for it: a ping from a tank that has fired off its shells shows where a life would pay most.
as_target: You see the followers trailing their leader. They are frail, and every one you kill is a buff that never happens.
A follower walking to its spot is marked and slow enough to shoot; kill it on the way and the offering fails.
When the flare goes off, back away for its few seconds; afterwards the enemy is a body short.
A feint that draws the sacrifice early leaves them with nothing for the real push.
teammates: Receivers gather in the ring when the leader calls it; those whose own card has a perk for it also get their own bonus, such as a reload, a repair or a helper.
Front-liners guard the followers, since the team's next buff walks with them.
A transport can carry the followers so they arrive alive, and a carrier that spends them from range is a variant.
On the enemy side, splash and anti-infantry players get a job: thin the followers before the push.
controls: Move with WASD and aim with the mouse; followers trail you by themselves.
Hold Q to show a target ring at the cursor within a medium range, and release to send the nearest follower; it gives itself up on arrival.
Tap Q to spend the follower nearest to you on the spot where you stand.
Spend-yourself: hold Q for a full second, a guard against slips, and the unit is used up.
Middle mouse, the universal ping: teammates ask for the buff at their position.
feedback: The follower count shows as pips on the leader's HUD, and enemies can count the bodies themselves.
The follower that has been sent carries a marker and a thin line to its target ring, so both teams see what is coming.
A bright flare and a distinct sound when the life is spent; the ring stays drawn on the ground while the buff lasts.
Receivers get a buff icon with a timer, and a second icon when their own bonus fires.
changes_from_rts: In Tempest Rising the thralls are a free resource that buildings keep spawning and one commander spends in numbers; a player unit gets a handful that come back slowly, so each life is a real choice.

The RTS thrall is a unit of its own; here it is an AI follower of the leader, because a player who is the thrall would spend a whole life walking to die. The spend-yourself version is only for a very cheap unit with a fast rebuy.
Tempest Rising gives each kind of receiver its own bonus through that unit's own perk. On cards that is a perk the receiver rolls, and the base buff has to be worth having without one.

Dawn of War's executions take the life from the buffed squad itself. With a player as the squad leader, that is the spend-follower variant: the leader gives up one of their own followers to boost the rest.
RTS players spend units freely; shooter players hate losing a life. Pay score for the trade, and never let one player spend another player's unit.

team_play.notes: The giver trades a life for the group's moment, so receivers have to be in the ring and use the window, guards keep the followers alive, and the enemy coordinates to thin them first. Where receivers carry their own bonus perks, the team is built around the offering. No hook names a buff: protector covers the cut to damage taken and resupply the reload bonus.

notes: AI followers that trail the leader, walk to a target and can be shot on the way; this reuses the squad crew model.
The buff itself is the rally-allies effect; the bonus per receiver needs an event that each unit's own perk can listen to.
Stock rules: how followers come back, and what a leader with none left can still do.
Spend-yourself needs a hold to confirm, score that passes to the dead giver and a fast way back to the buy screen.
Cues: follower pips, the marker on the sent follower, the flare and the ring.
A strong area buff with instant reloads is a big swing; it has to be worth a life without deciding the fight alone.
If followers come back too fast the price is fake and the buff is always on; too slowly and the unit has one moment per life.
Spend-yourself can be used to feed or to grief, and several givers in a chain make a buff that never ends.
Killing followers denies the buff outright, so a splash-heavy enemy can shut the unit down.
Enemies must see how many lives the leader has left and where an offering is heading.
A bonus per receiver multiplies icons; show one shared buff icon and at most one extra.
The flare must not look like an attack that hurts.

variants.name: Spend a minion
variants.summary: Send a cheap minion to a chosen spot, where it gives itself up and buffs every ally in the area.

variants.name: Spend a follower
variants.summary: A squad leader gives up one of the squad's own members: the rest of the squad hits much harder for a short time and can't fall back until the buff ends.
variants.seen_in: Dawn of War Commissar (Execute); Dawn of War II: Retribution Commissar Lord (Inspire Courage)

variants.name: Spend yourself
variants.summary: The unit itself is used up: the player goes back to the buy screen and the team gets a bigger buff. Only for a very cheap unit.
variants.seen_in: Tempest Rising Enlightened, seen as the unit itself; Supreme Commander Aeon engineers (Sacrifice)

adds_weaknesses.why: Using it ends its own life: the player is back at the buy screen and the team is one unit short.

variants.name: A bonus per receiver
variants.summary: On top of the shared buff, each receiver adds a bonus set by its own perk: gun units reload, heavy units mend, support units gain a short-lived helper, scouts see farther.
variants.seen_in: Tempest Rising Consecration and the Veti units' Consecrated perks

variants.name: Offering from a carrier
variants.summary: The minions ride inside the unit and are spent from the rear onto a distant spot, so they can't be shot on the way; the carrier's hold is the stock.

variants.name: Feed the caster
variants.summary: The spent minion refills the spender's own energy or ability charges and gives nothing to the team.

adds_strengths.why: Refills its own energy on the spot by spending a minion, so its abilities come back sooner than their cost suggests.

variants.name: Last gift
variants.summary: No key: the minion gives itself up by itself when its owner goes down, to bring the owner back, or it buffs nearby allies whenever it dies.
variants.seen_in: Warframe Sentinel with the Sacrifice mod

variants.name: Friend or foe
variants.summary: The same button can fall on a weak enemy instead of one's own minion: no buff, but the victim is hurt and its squad fights worse for a while.
variants.seen_in: Dawn of War II: Retribution Commissar Lord (Inspire Terror)

adds_strengths.why: One spent life gives the whole group around it a strong boost at the moment it matters.

adds_weaknesses.why: Every use costs a body: its followers are its ammunition, and with none left it has nothing to give.

countered_by.why: Area damage kills the frail followers in a bunch before any can be spent.
Anything built to clear light targets thins the followers and with them the buffs.
Fast flankers pick off the follower sent out alone to its spot.

open_questions: Will Shamble Frontlines have player units with AI followers (the squad crew model)? This pattern needs them, or it exists only in the spend-yourself form.
Is giving up your own life for a team buff acceptable in a game where each life is bought? How cheap must the unit be, and what does the player get back?
Should receivers carry their own bonus perks, as Veti units do, or does everyone get the same buff?
How do spent followers come back: over time, at a spawn point, or for money?
May the same button be used on an enemy, as Dawn of War II's Inspire Terror allows?

shooter_fit.reason: A dramatic team moment with a clear price and a clear thing for the enemy to shoot. But it needs AI followers, or asks a player to give up a life, and both are rare in shooters: the one cousin found spends a companion drone to revive its owner.
